title: Concerns about multiple crises and COVID-19-related stress symptoms in Tyrolean children (Austria) during and after the pandemic
abstract: Abstract The multiple systemic crises of recent years have the potential to impact child and adolescent mental health. There is extensive evidence on short-term mental health declines during the COVID-19 crisis. However, research on post-pandemic consequences and the relevance of other crises is limited. Here, we combined parent and child perspectives to analyse COVID-19-related stress over time and its association with concerns about other crises. We used repeated cross-sectional surveys of parents in Tyrol, Austria, regarding their children’s (3–13 years) COVID-19-related stress symptoms (CATS-2) between 2020 and 2025 (N = 5,056 measurements). Children (7–13 years) participated in cross-sectional surveys about their symptoms (CRIES-13, N = 575) and concerns about different crises (N = 259) in 2025. Based on parent information, we identified a peak in children’s COVID-19-related stress symptom prevalence during the pandemic winters of 2020/21 and 2021/22. In 2025, parents reported no symptoms for 99% (95% CI [95.3, 99.7]) of preschool children. However, approximately 10% (95% CI [7.3, 13.5]) of then school-aged children had COVID-19-related stress symptoms according to parents. The post-pandemic survey of children corroborated prevalence rates identified in parent reports. Additionally, children reported concerns about different crises. Concerns about all crises were particularly prevalent in children with COVID-19-related stress symptoms. The findings point to the long-term significance of temporary crises for children. Children are concerned about themselves and others and may struggle to navigate the threat of multiple crises.
